metric-distance: Imagine marking the same flat floor in feet and then in metres. What changed about the floor itself?
If you know how much distance one grid step represents, what could you do with a ruler?
clock-time: A clock and a ruler can travel together. Which one records the quantity in the question?
Could two people give an event different time labels while reading the same clock as it passes?
local-free-fall: Imagine dropping a scale and an object together. Why might the scale show no push during the fall?
Would one short fall tell you how two widely separated falling objects move?
tidal-difference: Picture two drops falling toward the centre of a planet from slightly different places. Compare their directions.
If you relabel a map, what happens to the measured gap between the two falling objects?
flat-interval: Set the three space steps to zero for a clock at rest. Which sign is in front of the remaining term?
Try two ticks of a clock at one place. Does the part containing the time difference vanish?
metric-cross-term: Write the two possible orders of an x step and a y step in the sum. Which objects do those labels refer to?
Look for the repeated pair of terms. Do the pure x and pure y terms occur twice too?
proper-time-metric: Compare two clocks that leave together, follow different paths and meet again. What information does the path supply?
Whose clock is following the curved path in this problem? Could an ordinary clock travel alongside a light ray?
lower-an-index: Try a table with a nonzero entry away from the diagonal. Which input components enter one row’s sum?
Taking an absolute value discards a sign. What operations does the metric table actually ask you to do?
polar-connection: Draw a flat sheet with a polar grid and pick a point away from its centre. What happens to its radial directions around a circle?
Could the directions drawn on a curved grid change even on a flat sheet of paper?
covariant-derivative: A vector can genuinely change. Which part of the apparent change could come from the grid itself?
Compare correcting how directions are measured with measuring the motion of two nearby falling objects.
parallel-transport: Carry an arrow pointing the same way across a flat polar grid. Do its projections onto the grid directions stay the same?
Keep the ruler units fixed while rotating the coordinate axes. What happens to the numbers describing one arrow?
geodesic-equation: Imagine describing a freely moving stone on a rotating grid. Would the choice of grid matter only for a light ray?
Before inferring a push, ask whether the coordinate directions change along the path.
transport-loop: Draw the starting and returning arrows from the same dot. Compare their lengths and then compare where their tips point.
Check the rule at each step on the loop. Could the local rule hold even if the final comparison is surprising?
riemann-comparison: Setting the connection to zero at a point says something about that point’s grid. What does a tiny loop test beyond that?
If two freely falling objects change their separation, would relabeling the clock change that measurement?
ricci-contraction: Changing how smoothly a grid is drawn differs from adding entries of a table. Which operation made this smaller table?
Can different entries add to zero even when the entries themselves are nonzero?
scalar-curvature: One number summarizes many curvature entries. Think of two nonzero numbers whose sum vanishes.
Check what signs can occur when the metric weights are included in the sum.
tidal-curvature: Write the minus sign from the formula separately from the minus sign of K. What happens when you combine them?
Locate mass in the equation for relative acceleration. What physical quantity does ξ stand for?
stress-energy: Picture a fluid that presses on a wall in its own rest frame. Where is that pressure recorded?
Think about riding past the fluid. Would you measure a flow crossing your patch of space?
einstein-tensor: Keep the stated scalar curvature and inspect the sign of the time entry of the metric. Which signs multiply?
Copy the minus sign first, then insert the signed value of the metric entry in parentheses.
einstein-equation: Could the same total mass have two different arrangements or different motions? What does the equation use at each place?
Count labels on two different spacetime maps. What physical information would you still need about their contents?
local-conservation: Draw a small box with energy entering on one side and leaving on the other. What would a local balance count?
Local bookkeeping compares nearby places. What would let different places and times share one global energy definition?
newtonian-limit: The shortcut assumes a small correction to the time entry. What should you check before using it near a horizon?
Would changing a symbol’s name change the size of the physical effect that was left out?
schwarzschild-radius: Compare the star’s actual size with the radius you calculated. Which one tells you where its surface is?
Write the two radii in the same unit. Would their relative sizes change if you used kilometres?
static-clock: Think about a freely falling clock at that location and a clock trying to stay at one radius. Are they following the same path?
As a hovering observer approaches the horizon, what happens to the support needed to keep that radius fixed?
gravitational-redshift: Imagine a light source moving toward a receiver even far from a strong gravitational field. What could change about the crests arriving?
Two observers can count wave crests per second. Which measured number would they compare?
weak-light-bending: Find b in the bending formula. Is it a factor above the fraction line or below it?
Hold the mass fixed and move the light path farther away. Which part of the fraction now changes?
wave-strain: Sketch a ring of freely separated points before a plus wave passes. Which separations does the strain describe?
Watch horizontal and vertical separations during the same part of the wave cycle. Compare the directions of their changes.
cosmic-scale: The scale factor relates distances between objects following the large-scale expansion. What keeps the parts of an atom together?
Compare two tightly bound atoms made of different elements. Which shared property matters for this question?
cosmic-redshift: Look back at the small-redshift assumption. Would increasing z preserve the reason the shortcut worked?
A formula can use matching units and still be approximate. What size of z was assumed?
friedmann-rate: Which symbol tells you whether the universe is expanding, and which symbol labels the cosmological constant?
Write down the conditions printed beside this equation before interpreting H.
